utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, we had to start a bit late because of the technical preparations. Okay. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to everyone. May I have 65 ter 01549, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Mr. Philipps, good afternoon. While we are waiting for it to come up I'll ask you the following: Studying the reports of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you notice what problems the corps was up against, problems which were hindering its proper functioning and operation? Will you be familiar with these problems when I show them to you in the documents now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The extracts that I took from the many hundreds of documents that I looked at related to the structure of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and to the passage and reporting of information. So I do have some knowledge of the problems and the functioning, but not a detailed knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that this is dated the 29th of May, 1992, when the Army of Republika Srpska had just been established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that the date is the 29th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you enumerate the most frequent problems that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had in its functioning, especially in the functioning of communications, or do you want me to jog your memory by showing you documents? What would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't be able to enumerate the most frequent problems that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had during its functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3 of this document, please. Page 2 in English, please. Page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see where it says 130 men and could you please read what follows that, following stabilisation, and so on. [In English] "Enemy losses are around 130 men ..." [Interpretation] Can you read what follows after the bit I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. "Following stabilisation of our own ranks, we approached the realisation of two main tasks which are: "First: Mobilisation of men and forming of the Hadzici battalion infantry unit. We have difficulties with this task, because armed men are self-organised and disorganised with very deviant convictions concerning their and only their own home. "We plan to solve this problem gradually by reassigning the already existing groups that are in various combat and non-combat task forces to organic battalion task forces. This process can be easily settled administratively, but practical it entails much effort in informing and organising men. It is imperative" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look at the demands, number 2. Could you read out point 2 under the heading "demands."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point number 2: "As soon as possible procure the command of our battalion with devices that can secure sending and receiving of coded messages on relation battalion command of the Serb municipality of Hadzici with Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At our interview we agreed that the Territorial Defence was municipal and that our brigades later on were linked to the municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, the Territorial Defence was based on municipalities. I understood that later on the brigades were really part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and were cut away from their political control by the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But there were quite a few problems before that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially it may have appeared that the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was trying to gain appropriate control of the brigades that had originally been part of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You noticed that everyone wanted to defend only their own home and that the psychology of these men from the people was territorial and strictly local; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the first extract that I have read from this document, that I read out earlier, it says that the men are self-organised and that they are concerned only with their own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D317.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 65 ter 12189, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for it, Mr. Philipps, I'll ask you the following: Did you notice how long the front line covered by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a relatively long front line, but I, at no time, made an attempt to measure it or to work out the exact length of that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I tell you that it was 240 kilometres long, does that sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I would have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the city itself the front line running between the houses and through the houses was 42 kilometres long and that by the end of the war the Muslims had stretched it out to 64 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with your figures because I don't know the answer, so I can't agree or disagree with your estimates of the length of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you would certainly agree that if it's 240 kilometres that it's very difficult for communication and for control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the organisation is at the centre of that line, then the communication is on what is called in military terms internal lines and is a much easier form of communication than a communication on external lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to read out -- well, let's look first. This is the 5th of March, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the date of the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the command of the Vogosca Brigade. Do you know where the Vogosca Brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vogosca Brigade was to the north of Sarajevo in the region of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to read out only number 1, point 1 here.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point number 1: "Create a mail and courier service in the command of the brigade to deliver mail and financial resources between the command of the SRK and the command of the brigade. "The headquarters administration will designate a courier, a vehicle for delivering the mail and an armed escort. "Mail will be delivered between the SRK command and the brigade command on every Thursday of the week. "Start implementing this order as of 11th of March, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that by the 5th of March, 1993, this brigade did not have either wire or other communications with the corps command and had to rely on couriers to establish communication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears from this document that the courier service was to be started on the 11th of March, 1993. I cannot deduce from that what the method of communication was before March 1993. However, as I understand it, at a particular point in time the Vogosca Tactical Group or Vogosca Operational Group was formed in order to improve communications to the north of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 65 ter 12416, please, 12416.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The document, Mr. Philipps, refers to the activities pertaining to putting the Army of Republika Srpska in order. So could you please read this brief passage: [In English] "Pursuant to your document strictly confidential number..." [Interpretation] and so on. That's the passage I mean.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to your document strictly confidential number 20/15-789 of 3 July 1993 and in accordance with the order of the Republika Srpska Army strictly confidential number 03/8-57 of 18 June 1993 on the creation of operative records of combat-readiness of units, you were obliged under item 3 of our order to forward a copy of operative records by the 15th of July, 1993, so that the SRK command could put the cards in order by the 20th of July, 1993, and forward them to the VRS GS. "Please urgently forward the operative record cards by the 20th July, 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it follow from this document that almost a year and a half or 15 months after the outbreak of the war, the corps was still struggling to establish good record-keeping?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a good example of staff work in order to improve the communication within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The staff officer is clearly trying to make sure that the combat-readiness information is available on each of the units and is ensuring that they pass the information up the chain of command so that he can view the combat-readiness state of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we see that this is the summer of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date, yes, is 18th of July, 1993. One might surmise that there was some other method of not using cards before that time. Combat reports were still passed up through the chain of command and information on combat-readiness was still passed up through the chain of command before the 18th of July, 1993. This document is really looking at improving the method of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will be Exhibit D319.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 15654, please. I hope there is a translation because this is a Prosecution document. Is there a translation? If not, we'll use what we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, you have sufficient familiarity with our language to see that this is an expose by the Chief of Staff at the analysis of combat-readiness, assessing the morale of units of the 4th Corps for 1991, so that was still the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, my knowledge of B/C/S is only sufficient to be in a restaurant or order a beer, but not technical military language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you can trust me and the interpreters can check what I say, but this is an expose of the Chief of Staff for 1991. So let's see what the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps inherited from the JNA and let's see what the situation was when it was established.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may we have page 2, please, the bottom half of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will mentioned only some of the more important tasks that were not realised this year. So they had to desist from their plans. First command staff war exercise of the corps command, manoeuvres. Secondly, a trip by the commander. So that corps did not do all these things, they gave up on them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please. The fifth from this page, which means the sixth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see what it says here, "planning": "In my assessment planning as one of the most important functions of command and control has put in place the preconditions for the carrying out of regular and extraordinary tasks." And then it goes on to say: "There are still subjective weaknesses in the domain of planning. The most important of these being, one, insufficient co-ordination among the command organs in the process of planning." And at the very bottom it says: "An especially big problem is in the poor manning of the commands and units, so with soldiers and officers, which is impacting most heavily on commands classified as 'R' who are carrying out their tasks with the minimum number of men and officers."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. If Mr. Karadzic would perhaps slow down his speech for the interpreters. Because we don't have a translation of this document, I think it's important for the translation to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the interpreters would be able to locate from where he is reading out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that was page 6 -- no, this is not page 6. It's page 7. So we are now on page 7. Towards the bottom of page 7 "Control and offering assistance": "Control and assistance to subordinate units were carried out according to plan, but there were still certain weaknesses such as non-executions of ordered activities by the subordinate commands and the repetition of the same omissions and weaknesses from one control to another." Secondly, a lack of a unified approach and the criteria in work and assessments of the situation in the units by the command teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Philipps, that even the JNA started to have weaknesses because of the events in Yugoslavia and because of the lack of military conscripts, the absence of military conscripts of Croatian and Muslim ethnicity so that even this army, which was the fourth strongest in Europe, was experiencing great difficulties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment on the document in front of me, but I can't answer questions about the weaknesses in the JNA before the events in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, does this document show that the weaknesses were already there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that the corps command was analysing all the weaknesses and problems that were occurring within the corps and appears to be addressing them. Any army unit would be continually reviewing its capabilities, continuing reviewing its level of training, and any army unit that didn't do this one would consider to be in some sense ineffective. This document shows how effective the staff were at analysing the problems, at thinking about how they could be corrected, at looking at the training that could be given to improve the command and control, at looking how the troops could be better trained, better equipped, and better accommodated. So to me this shows effective command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, at this moment I wanted to remind you of your obligation to diligently see to it that all the MFI documents would be translated and report to the Chamber so that they can be finally admitted. So it is your responsibility to see to it that they are translated. And one further matter is that some -- my understanding is that there are various video-clips you tendered into evidence during the course of your cross-examination. It is also your duty to tender the copies of the CDs that contains that video-clip to the Chamber. Please bear that in mind and let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope that the translation unit will do this. We have commissioned quite a number of translations, but they have to be verified. Can we have 15756, 65 ter. We received this from the OTP so I believe there must be a translation. Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is dated, you will agree, the 13th of July, 1994. The command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is sending this to all units and all the units and all the command posts of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the 13th of July, 1994. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- if the translation is correct that what you said is true -- so I'm hard-pressed to agree with a document that's in a foreign language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I believe there's a translation of this now available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the magic touch of Mr. Reid. Thank you. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to read the last page of the first task -- or rather, the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- of the first task, task 1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to read task 1? Is that what I'm reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Special attention should be given to the command and control on all levels. Orders and information should reach soldiers through commanders of battalions, companies, platoons, squads, and units, and that should be determined by controlling the commands and by giving them a task to train lower levels of command. "Dead-line: Permanent task."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see that as early as 1994 at lower command level they were still short of trained staff and these officers had to be trained in the course of the war; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's -- from that particular paragraph, there's no mention of the previous training. There's simply mention of the fact that training should go down to all levels. I can't see anywhere in that paragraph that mentions that the training so far was inadequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At lower levels of command to be trained for command, so that at the lower level of command they didn't have fully trained officers. Does that follow from this document, that they still had to be trained?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Training is a permanent task throughout the military. I can't think of any point in my time where I wasn't involved in either training others or being trained myself. It's continuous. And as it says here, "permanent task," this is something that is ongoing and continuous within a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And look at task 2, please, "it should be forbidden ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It should be forbidden for all unauthorised persons to sign report" -- I apologise. "... to sign report and documents that are not under their jurisdiction for the commander. "Dead-line: Permanent task."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the next page, task 12. Page 12, it's probably on the next page in English -- point 12, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Point 12: "To work permanently on the improvement of discipline and of the responsibility of all communications officers, as well as on the improvement of their training. To reduce (to eliminate) all negligence regarding connections to human factor. "Dead-line: Permanent task."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 34, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read out point 34, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With all respect to problems, the army's control and command should endure in developing of internal organisation, responsibility, order, and discipline, respecting of the law, level of training and skills, safety, good relations between people, and the image of Serbian soldier as presumptions of stable morale and entire values in implementing the combat goals."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go two pages further on, please, 39 and 42. It's the next chapter so the numbers start from 1 again. Next page, please. It's page 5 in Serbian. 42. This is 43 here. 39. [In English] "Priority reinforce ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read out 39, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. 39: "Priority reinforcement of PVL for key duties should be asked, in order to remove any weakness within control and command. "Dead-line: 30th of July, 1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. PVL is, is -- it's actually military personnel, right -- oh, professional military personnel, right, that's it. So in 1994 he is asking for professional military personnel to be involved, which is to say that that was not the case up until then or at least there weren't enough of them. Do you agree that this caring commander has many problems at that point in time that he has to resolve?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which commander signed this document. I haven't seen the end of the document. Is it the corps commander at that time that has signed the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at that -- by this date that is still General Galic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, therefore, agree with your description of him as a caring commander. I agree that he's attempting to resolve problems relating to reinforcement and the training of - as we called them yesterday - specialist officers who are normally full-time officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this only partial translation of the document? From number 27 it goes to number -- point 39 and then 40. Can I see the original one. Can you scroll up. Can we see the previous page of the B/C/S. The same is true in the original. I take it -- unless it is objected to, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D321, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter number 15891. Fine. We have a translation as well. The next page in Serbian, please. The next page in Serbian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is a document that was issued on the 19th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to read the following: "We have information ...," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We have information indicating that the enemy is preparing for actions and planning activities against the forces of the corps. In order to thwart their actions and intentions, I hereby order ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the rest, we can all read that. But this bit, "all officers and soldiers." I'll read it: [In English] "All officers and soldiers are to be removed from their homes and taken to the area of their position in combat." [Interpretation] And the next one: "Commanders," as in komandirs and komandants, "have to be in their units as envisaged, not at their homes." Do you see that? [In English] "Commanders must be in their units as foreseen and not at home." [Interpretation] Can we have the next page: "Commanders of the 3rd MAP and 4th" -- I'll read it. [In English] "The commanders of 4th MAP ..." [Interpretation] Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read that: "The commanders of the 4th MAP," abbreviation, "combined artillery regiment, and the 4th MPOAP," abbreviation, "combined anti-armour artillery regiment, must inform me of their whereabouts (not home or office). "The troops in the SVC," that is, Slavisa Vajner Cica and SPS Slobodan Princip Seljo Barracks must take care of the defence of facilities."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last one: "Check that there are no drunken soldiers and officers. And if there are such officers and soldiers, they should be detained straight away." Does this confirm what I put to you, that this was a people's army that lived at home and that goes to the front line in shifts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we go back to the paragraph about the commanders of the 4th MAP and the 4th MPOAP, those officers, as I understand it, were ex-JNA officers. And he's -- the commander is asking to be informed about their whereabouts. You could infer that they had spent time at home or in their office, but it's not clear that that's what they had been doing. The line about drunken soldiers and officers, I'm sad to say, is a continual problem with military. It occurs all the time and throughout most military organisations and is punished, as is said here, with drunken soldiers being subject to military discipline. I would have to go back and read the previous paragraphs again to remember what was precisely said about the individuals being at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page, page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "All soldiers and officers should be taken out from their homes and should be brought to the area where their positions are." And then, "Commanders have to be in their units as envisaged, rather than at their homes."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly in this point there has been a problem with not all the troops being in the places they ought to be and this has been recognised and measures being taken and, in fact, here is quite a list of orders making sure -- covering all sorts of matters relating to launching aerial bombs to driving around, loitering, avoiding duty, placing anti-tank obstacles, a whole series of things to improve the fighting capabilities of the corps. So in that sense, this is -- this is a continuation of improvements throughout the corps. And yes, I agree with you, does represent the fact that there were problems as you'd expect through any corps that had been fighting for such a period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I asked you to speculate what the objective of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was. You said that your speculation was that it may have been the blockade of Sarajevo. If I tell you that there were a bit less than 200.000 Serbs living in Sarajevo along with declared Yugoslavs 157.000 and that the corps had 19.000 men all the way up to 23.000 men when the level of mobilisation was the highest, do you agree that that is over 10 per cent mobilisation, up to 15 per cent actually?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the 200.000 Serbs living in Sarajevo were -- that's 200.000 male individuals, in which case 20.000 would, indeed, be 10 per cent mobilisation of 200.000. But as I understand it, females were not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, no. That was the general population. I'm talking about the general population -- well, I mean 30 per cent are able-bodied men, right, of military age?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm not an expert on statistics relating to demographics. I know that there are demographic experts, but I'm afraid I'm not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we are talking about the general population here, the mobilisation base is different. So it is less than 200.000. The number of soldiers is, say, between 18- and 20.000. Does that mean that that is about 10 per cent and even more in terms of the general population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that 20.000 is 10 per cent of 200.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you take into account that there were about 30.000 Serbs left in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, then it's even more than 10 per cent, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find it absolute waste of time. The witness is not in the position to confirm whether it was 200.000 or 300.000, whether it's 20.000. That calculation can be done by anybody if you establish the fact first. I don't think this is the witness who is suited to deal with this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Actually, I'd like to bring the witness to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now my question, Mr. Philipps: What is it that could compel this population to send every able-bodied male into the corps if it weren't for the protection of one's own homes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't put myself inside the head of other people, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, what you're asking the witness to do is to speculate, and one thing that is not evidence is speculation. I don't know whether you're going to go into an analysis of the charts which have been produced and which were the, as it were, the principal function of this witness's task. Because that seems to me -- unless you are going to challenge the accuracy of those charts in terms of what's actually on them, the other area of challenge might be an interpretive challenge as to what it means. And it seems to me that that may be the most useful way that this witness's time can be spent in assisting the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Of course formally speaking I am going to proffer a few corrections of this diagram or chart. However, as far as interpretation is concerned, creating an impression of a well-organised huge military force that is fighting an undefended city, I cannot leave the Trial Chamber deluded in that way. That is not the case. Mr. Philipps saw this from the documents that we read today and also the documents that he had read. Literally people did not wish to leave their homes. They defended their very often homes. So it is not the way things have been depicted. This is not a corps of an army that had come from somewhere. These were people who were mobilised right from there, and I have to say that this was a corps that was not operating properly because it had lots of problems. That is what I'm trying to prove through these documents that Mr. Philipps had seen or should have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I understand that's your position, Dr. Karadzic, but it's -- I don't -- Colonel Philipps, as he is properly to be addressed in the sense of the evidence which he's giving, I don't think, and he'll correct me if I'm wrong, has viewed his task as being that sort of an analysis or claims the expertise to answer that sort of a question. And if that's correct, then asking him that sort of question is simply taking up the time that you might usefully be using in analysing that which he does have expertise in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But may I remind the witness and the Trial Chamber that the witness had claimed that the flow of information functioned properly, whereas we see here in 1994 that a front line of 140 kilometres still had to be visited by a messenger, courier. This is not a modern way of communication. It is highly pain-staking. 12410 is the next 65 ter number that I'd like to have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, knowing the terrain around Sarajevo, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to comment on the accused's statement he made just now as to the flow of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a sense I would. The flow of information up and down the corps was evident throughout the period. The means of that communication at some times appears to have been runner or messenger or courier, and it might not be a modern method of communication. And the British army in times when communication fails and in my experience I have sent runners, I have had runners come to me. You use any means capable of passing information. That doesn't always mean a digital radio, it can frequently mean by motorbike or by hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue. 12410?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you do agree, Mr. Philipps, that your task was to portray how this corps functioned, especially from the point of view of its capacity to communicate and to ensure a flow of information; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My task was to show the organisation of the corps and the lines of command and control up and down the corps and the passage of data up and down the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's save time. We're going to leave this document aside. We're going to drop it all together.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And 01830, that's what we'd like to have. 1D08280. I have the English version here. I believe that one does exist there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to read the part that starts with: "In spite ..." I think we don't have a Serbian version, so just this sentence "in spite of ..." the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In spite of many warnings, during any group or individual visits to the bodies of SRK command, numerous weaknesses and defects has been found in the subjugated units."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the rest "order," "I order," number 1.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I order. "From the 12th of the 4th, 1993, at all levels of RiK and SRK, it is most strictly forbidden to deliver and consume alcohol during both working and extra time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Immediately and with no exception eliminate all defects in the system of tours of duty, particularly with the bodies that are directly connected to OC SRK command. In that sense, the special attention should be paid to the system of informing OC K-SRK and eliminate the weaknesses specially regarding the speed, completeness, and credibility of the information. "From now on every information must consist of the following: "Who is informing. "What has happened. "Time, place, consequences, and undertaken measures."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to read 3 and 4 as well.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "While informing the superior command, it is obligatory to strictly respect the authority and prevent any communication with unauthorised persons in SRK command. "Starting from the mentioned date it is the most strictly forbidden to perform any oral or written addressing to MS VRS Presidency of RS government, RS government and the presidents of Serb municipalities, that is, their bodies outside SRK command."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And 7.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Immediately upon receipt of this order ensure that all members of the unit must have an excellent appearance strictly in accordance with the temporary rules of the VRS. Special attention should be paid to elimination of the appearance of men with a long hair, beards, untidy moustaches, and holding any kind of designations except regular ones."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number 13, please, the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The commanders of the independent battalions, regiments, and brigades in the zones of their own responsibility will provide a maximum support to the actions of SRK command in arresting and eliminating the killers, thieves, burglars, and similar. In the own units and during the meetings with the soldiers and officers, it is obligatory to explain the role and character of this action and previously achieved results and specially underline an excellent reaction among the population."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 14, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In own units it should ensure that each its member is obliged to report to the bodies in charge and also other officers immediately the perpetrators of the criminal acts and war profiteer so that we could stop it once forever."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the second paragraph of paragraph 16, please. Can you scroll up a bit. It starts with: "All members ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "All members of the units must be particularly convinced that we not have munitions factory, oil sources, and the stores full of food, so that we can take only what we have. In own units it should prevent, by any mean, further transfer of the munitions, p/g and food."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 17, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Again and last time, I strictly forbid the movements of personnel from one unit to the other without permission of the commander and acceptance of those personnel by the commanders of the units to which they come."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Philipps, does this look like a people's army that needs quite a bit of discipline, that is lacking at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are certainly mentioned there lapses of discipline relating to dress and behaviour and all sorts of problems. The corps at this time had been fighting for a period of time, and you might expect under those circumstances there would be problems with behaviour, with equipment, with the appearance of soldiers. It's a continual effort of the command to maintain the standards of military discipline within a unit, and this represents an attempt, a continuation, to maintain that level of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the first page you saw that the type of information provided is prescribed, what happened, time, place, measures taken. Is this conceivable, this kind of document, a year into the war in a proper professional unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the first page again so that Mr. Philipps can be reminded of what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From now on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I'm not in the least surprised by order number 1. The military, including the British military, has strict rules about consumption of alcohol while on duty or on the lines. In areas of operations consumption of alcohol is forbidden. So that is a standard, I would say, a standard order. The second point really is relating to the nature of reporting and the list of information, who, what, when, where, and what you're doing about it is the format of a standard military report. This is a reminder to people to submit reports in a standard format. In my experience, even trained soldiers occasionally need to be reminded of the format of reports and how that reporting should be delivered so that it's understandable to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My point is that this shows how many problems a corps of a people's army has. A professional unit of this size would certainly not be facing this type of problem. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to put the place of a regular military unit into the situation that had occurred up until that period. The war, at that time of this order, had been being waged for a year, at least. If you have a single unit in combat continuously for a year, even a regular, professional unit would suffer difficulties and would require tight command and control. So I would expect any unit, any corps, brigade, that had been consistently in combat for a long period of time to have to work very hard to keep up its level of military discipline. And that's what this document appears to be. It is an order to ensure the maintenance of good order and military discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, do you by any chance know what RiK is the abbreviation of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it refers to another corps, but I could be quite incorrect. But I'm not sure of that abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist, it's command and control.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it to be one of the Defence documents in other cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Similar to the document yesterday, Your Honour, this is a Defence document from the Galic case. In this instance our quick check of the record shows that there is a B/C/S version; however, we would ask that the translation here be reviewed. There's a number of abbreviations that it's unclear what they mean and for the sake of accuracy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So far we admitted the documents with Defence translation which will be checked again later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that caveat we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm noting the time. We have five minutes until the break, but I'm -- I'd like to remind you of the time-limit we put for your cross-examination. Given the nature of the evidence Mr. Philipps gave in his chief and the questions you put during the cross-examination so far, we find that the five hours is more than sufficient. I'd like to remind you that the Chamber is not minded to extend any time for your cross-examination. So bear that in mind in the remaining for your time. You've spent so far about a bit less than four hours. So in the next session you will have 70 minutes to conclude your cross-examination. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll have to adjust to that, but I thought it was a good opportunity to get an overview of the corps. Can we have 1D01156.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Mr. Philipps, looking at the documents of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you notice to what extent the cease-fire was being violated -- all the cease-fires brokered by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work on any time-line or data relating to cease-fires, so I had no information of when a cease-fire was in operation and when a cease-fire had been broken. So that did not form part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we look at 2, at the very bottom. Everyone can read what these violations looked like. Yes, here it is. In Serbian it is number 2. In English it's probably the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read number 2: "The state of combat-readiness ..."?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The state of combat-readiness in corps units has been improved by the latest activities and combat results. It continues to be encumbered by ineffective command and control at almost all levels and the large influence of the authorities on command and control up to brigade level, especially in the Rajlovac Brigade, the 2nd Rmtbr, Romanija Motorised Brigade, and Vogosca Brigade. The tendency to defend one's own door-step is still present and it is very difficult to get units to move forward short distances, not to mention manoeuvres of units in the corps zone."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at: "The corps command and co-operation with the civilian authorities is taking measures ..."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The corps command is taking measures in co-operation with the civilian authorities and the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, to prevent negative occurrences. The measures have been slow and ineffective so far, and despite the seminar on Jahorina we do not have the same approach to resolving problems. It is noticeable that we agree in talks, but in practice everybody does what he wants."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this also show that this was a people's army and that it was hard to co-ordinate it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think this is showing the recognition of problems that are occurring, and certainly methods are being used to improve that. They've clearly had a seminar on Jahorina about the subject. So there are measures being taken to improve the difficulties. The -- those brigades that are having difficulties are identified individually. And again I'm not sure of the date of the document, but you might expect in such a situation that it would be difficult to get units to attack or move forward at that point in time due to the possibility of casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's dated 21st of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1992, so -- yes, quite early.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says here that he doesn't want to leave his home, not that he's afraid of getting killed? So he's acting locally; is that right? He wants to defend his threshold, that's the expression we use in our part of the world.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the tendency to defend one's own door-step as a phrase, not necessarily literally, but defending a particular area, and that appears to be a problem with these specific brigades. I was referring to the lack of willingness to go forward that is mentioned elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. This will be admitted as Exhibit D324. We'll now have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If this document has been admitted could we have 65 ter 11707, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record this has been admitted as P1003. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When did we pass 1.000? Can we -- oh yes, we do have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see the date is the 21st of July, 1992. There is quite a lot of information in this document, but I would like us to look at page 3 because it refers to the topic you are dealing with. Page 3 and it's the same in English, is it? "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps" -- I'm not sure, it's on page 3. "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is holding the defence lines" -- I believe it's the next page in English. Could you read -- very well, I'll read it: "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps firmly -- is firmly holding the line of defence of the largest part of Serbian Sarajevo and is successfully controlling the territory in their area of responsibility." This was now called east Sarajevo, and do you know that at the time the Serbian neighbourhoods in Sarajevo in the suburbs organised themselves as Serbian Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to comment on the document or on your comment on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, what I just said about the existence of Serbian Sarajevo. The document isn't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hadn't heard that it was called -- I'd heard of the concept of Serbian Sarajevo. I did not know that that area defended was called Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now it exists as a town, but it's called east Sarajevo because our neighbours don't like it being called Serbian Sarajevo. That's for everybody's information. Can we look at this passage which says the Herzegovina Corps and where it begins with the words "in question," the next passage. Could you please read this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think Mr. Philipps is able to read that passage. Why does he have to read out that passage, unless it is that necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From the previous passage on the territory of the Serbian republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina there are certain weaknesses which if they are not dealt with quickly can influence the morale of the units and then: "Primarily it's a question of the non-functioning or poor functioning of the state institutions and organs, and this is significantly burdening the work of the units' commands and the army." Do you see that all this is in the in the process of being set up and that it's functioning with a great difficulty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the date of this document, the hostilities had only just begun in Sarajevo and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was in the process of organising itself and sorting out command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are informed that this has been already admitted, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, that's 1003. All right. Thank you. May we have 65 ter 1781. 65 ter 1781. It's quite a voluminous document, analysis of combat-readiness from April of 1993 and there is a translation, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We've seen the front page, analysis of the combat-readiness and activities and so on for 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the front page of a document that has been prepared at army level by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 32 in Serbian and the chapter heading is "Radio Communications." We have the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I think it's page 33 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page. This is "Radio-relay Communications," and then we have "Radio Communications" on the next page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the passage which begins: "At brigade level."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English it might be on the next page 35. [In English] "At the brigade battalion level."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to read that passage.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the brigade-battalion level and down to platoon level, radio communication is the fundamental command and control communications link. However, there are quite a few problems at this level using this type of communication. One of the basic problems is the fact that units of this rank do not have appropriate low power equipment. Supplying energy sources to operate the equipment is no less a problem. A large number of users do not properly use portable low capacity equipment and hand-held Motorolas, two-way hand-held radios. These are also susceptible to interception and interference on the part of the enemy, and the users fail sufficiently to use general cryptoprotection documents."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we now look at the first passage under the heading "Wire Communications." The first three paragraphs under the heading "Wire Communications."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Wire communications at the Main Staff - first subordinate commands level, have not been greatly used because of the disruption of these on the main routes. "The use of such communication links at the corps-brigade level have also been quite difficult owing primarily to the great distances and poorly developed SVZL, expansion unknown, and cable lines, particularly in hilly and mountainous areas. "At the brigade-battalion (artillery battalion) level and down to the platoon, and in front line positions, this type of connection is the principal communications link. "However, all Army of Republika Srpska units have made maximum use of an integrated wire service and PTT links by linking up with the nearest PTT communications centre. "The corps uses PTT communication links ranging from 10 PTT connections in the Herzegovina Corps to 93 PTT connections in the Eastern Bosnian Corps, as shown in the following table."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come across this information pertaining to the difficulties of wireless and wire communications in the Army of Republika Srpska and also in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read this analysis and seen this analysis before. As I understood it, the wire communications at the lower level was the principal link, that is, from brigade to battalions. However, their radios were not functioning at an appropriate level. The corps to the Main Staff communication functioned very effectively using teleprinters, as is mentioned on the previous page. So what is happening is that command and communication is maintained by whatever means. So where radio is not available, wire is used. Where wire is not functioning, they're using the local PTT, the telephone network, as a means of communicating. So they're using whatever means are available. When radios don't work, they use wire, when wire doesn't work, they use Motorolas, hand-held radios. So there's an attempt to make sure that communication is functioning, but it is not the -- it's not the perfect communication by any means and it is not the same type of communication that you would expect to find throughout a professional corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That said, if my memory serves me correct, radio communications are the bane of any army's life, particularly when they get wet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It would be fair to ask a current serving soldier how he felt about modern communications, for example, in Afghanistan, to see whether even the British army had appropriately functioning communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Which is why there are still runners.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say here that they're short of equipment and so on and when it comes to wire communications they say that the lower down one goes the poorer the communications. So at the level of the Main Staff and the corps, communication is functioning well; but between the brigade command and the battalion and company commands, there are all sorts of problems, both in radio communications, wire communications, and so on, because of the mountains, because of damaged main roads, and so on. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the communication is not perfect and all types of means were used to try and establish communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have three pages further along, it's 35 in Serbian and the heading is the situation in the organs and units of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it to come up, I remember our conversation when you confirmed that most information is passed from brigade and battalion level up to brigade level, and from brigade level up to corps level. And the further up one goes, the more the information is summarised and reduced to the most essential points; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. At each level the information is summarised so that the commanding officer or the commander of the formation receives the correct amount of data and isn't overwhelmed by detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we see that communication on these two sides has the least possible equipment, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We see that the communications up to the corps level are better, but at lower level, brigade level, communications are poorer than at higher levels; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems from the description here that the level of, let's call them electronic radio communications and wire communications were poorer. But you have to remember that a company commander would see his battalion commander every day, and a battalion commander in such situation, in such an area may very well see his brigade commander every day. Much harder for a brigade commander to visit the corps command post, and so the important communication is between the brigade and the corps -- and the corps up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in English, please. And in Serbian it's the right page. It has to do with personnel levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us just see where the personnel levels are. [In English] "Understaffing." [Interpretation] Can you read the paragraph starting with "understaffing"? It's towards the top of the page, "understaffing" --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it: "Understaffing in respect of key duty officers such as heads of signal corps, signal company, and signal" -- I'll start again. Sorry. "Understaffing in respect of key duty officers such as heads of signals corps, signals company, and platoon leaders, as well as the lack of certain critical specialities such as radio-relay operators, UPF, and radio-relay mechanics, radio teleprinter operators, automatic telephone, and TT exchange mechanics, all affect the communications system and the battle readiness of signals units generally and the signals branch as a whole. One of the problems is also the unresolved status of civilians formerly serving in the JNA and now in the VRS. There is presumed to be a surplus of them which is in fact not the case, as they perform work for which we have no replacements."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this complete the picture regarding these difficulties that exist in communications between different levels within the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have seen that in all specialisms, engineering, artillery, communications, that there was a shortage of highly trained personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Exhibit D325.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1815, could we have that, please. It's a map, a map that had been marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have kindly confirmed that on the basis of the documents of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps you managed to see what the deployment of forces was in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps one map so that it would be bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this look familiar to you? Is it Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be an oblique -- I'd rather not call it a map. It's more of an appearance of a satellite picture or an aerial photograph of Sarajevo showing locations and blue and red dotted lines that approximate the lines during the conflict. But I can't see a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the lower left-hand corner do you see Ilidza Serbian part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the title of this document in e-court suggests, this is an annotated version of a map. I have two issues here. The first is where those annotations come from. It looks very similar to a map that was presented to a previous witness or Mr. Karadzic asked that previous witness to make annotations, which brings me to my second point. You will recall after that witness made those annotations you asked the Prosecution to come to an agreement with the accused about the positions. I can inform the Chamber that no agreement was reached. One of the reasons for that is what we see before us is not, in fact, a map but is a satellite photograph. It's a visual aid for the Chamber. We're willing to come to an agreement on detailed maps that are on our 65 ter list. For example, we could come to an agreement on the breakdown of map number 1 in the Prosecution's map book, and we can certainly come to an agreement on geographical locations. If the -- if Mr. Karadzic is concerned about coming to agreement on the elevations of those positions, we can certainly do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you have time to analyse this aerial image, in particular whether or not you agree with the geographical name of those locations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We haven't analysed every single position, but I can give you one example. We didn't come to an agreement on the position of Grdonj, for example, at the top of the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure it was appropriate to hear that in the presence of the witness, but -- so there are certain areas you cannot agree as to the exact location of those places?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean -- I was going to respond because I was present at the time that I believe this was created and I would just add one additional point. It is correct, we could not come to an agreement on that, and I would simply note that I think it -- if the Court refers back to the testimony, I think it was clear that this was prepared with considerable guidance by the accused and considerable trepidation and misgivings by the witness who was placing markings on there. So to call it a map indicating locations I think would be misleading in contrast to what it appears to be, which is some dialogue between the accused and the witness at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it this aerial image, marked image, was produced by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The underlying map is map number 2 in our map book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, the aerial image that we are seeing now with the red -- with markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The yellow markings are, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then I think I can -- I gather the Prosecution can come up with a suggestion, another suggestion, bearing these places on this image? And then we can see the difference between position of the Defence as well as the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We're happy to use, for example, 65 ter 09390B and C. That's two booklets. The first one -- and we've provided these to the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No -- but I take it these are places the Defence wants to locate in this aerial image, and you can tell us whether you agree with certain locations and you do not agree -- you can indicate the places as to which you do not agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The problem is, Your Honour, we don't agree with placing these images on an aerial image. It's not a map. So we can't place GPS co-ordinates, for example, on an aerial image. This was provided merely as a visual aid for the Trial Chamber to understand the general topography of Sarajevo. It's not appropriate to put accurate geographical locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is your position that you're not able to indicate where Vogosca is in this aerial image?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Only very generally, not a pin-point location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Defence is intending to pin-point that Vogosca is at that point. So I would recommend to continue your dialogue, conversation, between the Defence to assist the Chamber. If the Chamber is able to see where Vogosca is in this aerial image, it will be -- the Chamber will benefit -- not only from -- as well in addition to the map. But, first of all, we would expect that the parties can agree to name these -- spot these places on the map first, and then we can see how we can go from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when you say "on the map" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The map you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The detailed map in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The detailed map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's not going to be very difficult to transpose from the map to the photograph. I mean, the places are either identifiable on the map or they're not, and some are obviously self-evident, like for instance the airport. So I don't think it's as much of a problem as you feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I agree generally. It's not as simple as you make out with respect to the confrontation lines and where those appear on the aerial image. It's just not as accurate as you would find on a map rather than a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No, I accept that, that that's to do with projection as much as anything else. But we're really I think looking at place names rather than exact positions of front lines. But perhaps we've spent enough time on this already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that caveat, let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I just remind you of the fact that we did not produce this map, it was the OTP. We didn't make the markings. We did not even challenge the confrontation lines. It's the Prosecution that marked them. We did not mind because this is a schematic -- or no, it's not a schematic, but it's not precise enough. However, what is precise enough is that this is the hill of Hum and Mr. Harland confirmed that, that also that this is Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo, Colina Kapa, and that it was held by the Muslim forces. He also confirmed that this was Grdonj, it can be nothing else but this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is no point continuing that debate. But it is the Defence that put that mark in yellow, Hum, or Vogosca, or Zuc?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was confirmed by Mr. Harland. I asked him what was where and whether he agreed, and he confirmed that those were the positions concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it was confirmed or not is a matter to be analysed by the Chamber, but let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you find your way on this map, Mr. Philipps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the oblique aerial photograph in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise these localities, the ones that were marked here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of them I do recognise, the shape of the roads, the airport, the river quite clear on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see Nedzarici, the place that you had marked on the previous map; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the yellow name, Nedzarici, with a yellow dot and an arrow pointing to a specific place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the hill of Mojmilo and does this correspond to what you know of Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mojmilo is generally in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Nedzarici is in the Serb red line and Mojmilo in the Muslim line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see where Lukavica is? It hasn't been marked here, but it can be seen on this image. It is to the east of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a yellow marking for Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what is your question to this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask Mr. Philipps how much time we need to go from Lukavica to Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the distance involved in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking of a direct line from Lukavica to Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To measure that, I would require a map. An oblique photograph has a different scale. The nearer you are to the bottom of the photograph, to the top of the photograph -- so, for example, a centimetre at the top of this picture would represent a different distance to a centimetre at the bottom of the picture. So really to measure distances, one requires a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Karadzic asked you the distance as the crow flies. He asked to go from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To go round the lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
