utterances.text: Yes. Without seeing the map of all the lines except bearing in mind what I saw from the map we had yesterday, you would have to travel I think in a clockwise direction round Sarajevo, so many, many tens of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that it's not more than one kilometre; however, do you know that we had to go 100 kilometres to Lukavica from Nedzarici, 110 kilometres, all the way around from Nedzarici to Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the ABiH forces within Sarajevo are fighting on interior lines, and in this case the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is fighting on exterior lines and therefore communication in that area would be much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see that on the basis of the agreement, according to which we handed over the airport, we had the right to use the runway for our wounded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read data relating to agreements either between VRS and ABiH or at political level or with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the report you saw where the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were. Do you agree that the forces of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were not at Mojmilo, at Hrasno, at Debelo Brdo, at Colina Kapa, at the Jajce barracks, Grdonj, Hum, Kobilja Glava, Zuc, and Sokolje?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, but mostly I admit from the map we saw yesterday, that those areas fall within the lines of the ABiH. But certainly there's confusion about -- let me pick an example. Zuc on the map here is shown as a single dot. Zuc is a large hill. Hum is a large hill. Mojmilo covers several hundred square metres, and Debelo Brdo covers several hundred metres and Grdonj. All of these are large areas if marked by an individual dot, it's somewhat misleading. So I would be hard-pressed to say that the whole of a particular place, for example, Rajlovac on this map is shown as being on the SRK side, but parts of Rajlovac perhaps, according to this map, are also held by the ABiH. So to say that a specific place from the data on this map is held by one side or the other might be misleading, whereas some places are clearly held entirely by one side or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agree that the mountaintops that I mentioned were in the hands of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I just answered that question. I can't agree that the whole of particular places are held. I would not want to say that the whole of Hrasno Brdo were held by one side or the other without seeing what extent we think Hrasno Brdo covered; when, in fact, here it's shown only as a dot on the map, in the same way that I don't know the exact boundaries of Grbavica and whether Debelo Brdo is considered to go further up the hill or not. You would really have to ask a local Sarajevan what part of the town he considered to be the whole of Hum. I spent nine months there, so I'm not the person to ask about the detailed topography and locations within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the documents that you did see showed you who was firing and from where, and here you can see that that is in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So from that point of view a millimetre here, a millimetre there, do we agree that these mountaintops are mentioned in reports as places from where there is firing? Remember the reports, Sokolje, Zuc, Hum, that there was firing coming from there and from Grdonj, from Colina Kapa, all of these elevations around Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many, probably not all of these places, are mentioned within the reports. Again, I did not look at the reports with detailed information about the location of where fire was coming from or who the firing was at, nor did I mark on a map the locations of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. My purpose of my report was to show the structure of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and not locate its position on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, shall we ask the witness to initial this or shall we deal with this with someone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no point for the witness to sign this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then we can remove this map -- however, let's keep it because Mr. Harland had kindly confirmed to us that these were the names of these elevations. If the other side wants us to spell this out in more specific terms, my associates are available to them and they can go into every little millimetre. 1D1 -- or actually, 1D0185. Could we have that now, please. 1D01825.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Philipps, you were an OTP investigator as well, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think my CV covers the time that I worked for the OTP as a military analyst, not as an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was it that you analysed in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked on -- originally directed by Mr. Ierace the structure of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Before that I worked on financial data relating to the former President Milosevic. A whole series of matters for the OTP. I worked on the Dubrovnik shelling case. I worked on the prosecution of General Dragomir Milosevic relating to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I worked on various mapping projects relating to the weapons used in Dubrovnik and I worked on identifying equipment and the capabilities of equipment for various cases, a whole series of military analytical tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not testify in the trial of General Milosevic; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, I did not testify in that matter. The chart, however, I produced may very well have been used by the Prosecution in understanding the structure of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, even if that structure was not used in the prosecution itself as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It also has to do with the structure of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, not only the flow of information; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My chart really shows the command and control structure and the way the organisation is put together. It's sometimes called an order of battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your capacity of investigator, did you interview anyone for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I'm racking my brains now to think of all the people I interviewed. I must have interviewed over 30 or 40 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is considerable investigation work, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was usually working in conjunction with an investigator, that is, a trained policeman. He would conduct the interviews and I would assist from the point of view of military analysis. Most of the interviews that I was assisting with related to military personnel, either United Nations monitoring officers, members of the ABiH, or members of the VRS. And in some cases JNA -- former JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were these high-ranking officers and commanders such as Smith, Rupert Smith? He was a general, Mr. Koenig? Which of the high-ranking people did you interview?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- let me think. I interviewed General Rose, I interviewed General Smith, General Karavelic, and various other senior officers. But I don't know how much -- I don't know what I'm able to say from the OTP's point of view. If you wanted a full list, I think -- a full list of when and how those interviews took place, I don't know whether that's something the OTP would provide or could provide. That might be of more use to you if you wanted to know more about my background. But in a sense you're testing my memory of five years ago, ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure where this line of questioning is going, but obviously to the extent that it doesn't relate to Mr. Philipps' analysis of the SRK, the review he's conducted for the purpose of this trial, I don't think he should get into internal matters of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's very important for us to know to what extent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Put your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your task in these interviews that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- my task within each interview was different. For example, if interviewing personnel who were related to the technical use of mortars, then my job would be to assist the investigator in understanding some of the technical data and the capabilities of the weapons, for example, the noise signature, the flash signature, the range of the weapon, the use of mortar tables, the types of ammunition, and this sort of thing. Where we were interviewing a senior officer, then I may have assisted in helping the investigator understand the relationship between a platoon, a company, a battalion, and a brigade, as these are not terms that civilians readily understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read the indictments -- or rather, did you read the indictments in the cases in which you were involved during the interviews?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you glean information from these indictments and were you guided by them in what you should be looking for, what you should be investigating?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not responsible for leading the investigation; that was the job of the investigator. My role was to advise on technical military matters. From that point of view I was simply providing technical data, not -- not directing the investigating by any means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were guided by the information provided in the indictments, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be fair to say that as a military analyst the indictment is one thing which one tends to put on one side as an analyst and then see what information the investigator requires from you as an analyst. So I wasn't directed in any particular way by the indictment. I would be directed by the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were some sort of consultant or assistant in investigating a phenomenon or a person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose consultant is perhaps a term you could use. An intelligence analyst or military analyst is maybe a better term. I answered technical military questions, tried to explain in layman's terms complex military matters; and so in that sense, yes, a consultant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What then did you do during the interview with General Smith?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the interview with -- cast my mind back to the interview with General Smith which was in London at the Ministry of Defence, I typed the notes contemporaneously with the interview and then assisted the two lawyers and the investigator understand some of the answers so they could then ask further questions of General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you were part of a team. What participants did you interview on your own?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a military analyst, it would not be normal to interview an individual on my own, although I do have -- I have been trained in interviewing skills, I do not have the interviewing skills of a trained investigator, a policeman. So I would only ever assist in interviews, not conduct the interview on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did your interventions and your instructions enter into the investigator's report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where'd I'd been able to assist the investigator, it might make his report clearer or might make the -- might change the questions that he asked. A good example might be when interviewing about a technical matter relating to combat, I might be able to clarify what had occurred so the investigator could understand what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were integrated in the OTP to quite a large extent, were you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military analysis team was part of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at this document. You mentioned this person, Vaska, and I say that he was some sort of scout and that he was under command and that a disciplinary measure was instituted against him. Is this evident from this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It appears that this is a report to the Main Staff of the VRS from the deputy commander, Dragomir Milosevic, relating to an occurrence, some conduct of the individual listed here Vaska, and it's been agreed that he will not be arrested and that the corps command has decided for the time to file a criminal charge against Vaska and make him responsible for any further -- it's the English that -- it's got me. And to -- yes, and to make sure that he doesn't actually make any further mistakes as far as I can see. It's a disciplinary document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you accept that this Vaska is the person you called Vidovic? His last name was Vidovic? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that the individual mentioned here is the same as the individual on my chart. His full name is not listed on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. But you have Vaska Vidovic or Vasilije Vidovic in your diagram, do you not? Vaska's Platoon --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is shown on my diagram, but there are also lots of people called Dragomir and it doesn't mean it's the same person. It could be the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As an expert could you describe to us what happens when an army loses an important territory? Does it have to withdraw to the territory that remains to it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a sense by definition what you've said is the case. If it's lost the territory, then it has to withdraw, it's been pushed from that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the presence and density of that army on that territory then increase?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If its area of responsibility has contracted, there would be more troops within the area. That's, I suppose, simply a law of physics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that demobilisation of a large part of an army is a very complex and sensitive job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be true. That doesn't follow -- that's a non sequitur, if you like, from the last statement, that's a separate statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But if an army loses some of its territory, the war is not yet over, it's not time to demobilise; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question. It would not normally be the case for an army to demobilise unless a war was -- the war had concluded, peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But even when a war is over, is large-scale demobilisation a problem from the viewpoint of economic suffer, psychological, sociology, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak about my knowledge of events such as the Napoleonic War, the First World War, and the Second World War. And after any large-scale war, the demobilisation of troops causes a political and economic instability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the witness confirm anything about this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vaska is mentioned here, Vaska's Platoon, which is in the witness's chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When -- if my memory's correct, when he referred to Vasko's Platoon, it was "o" in Vasko not Vaska; is it not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may be simply to do with the ending in B/C/S. I think it's probably a case matter, but I can't say that this Vaska is the same as the Vaska or Vasko on my chart as it doesn't have his full name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I don't believe the witness has been able to add anything to this document. He hasn't been able to identify that it is the same Vaska. In any event, if this is the -- only the English version and we don't have the B/C/S original, we'd ask it to be MFI'd in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is also one of the Defence exhibits used in other case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: It appears, again, to be that case -- the Galic case number is in the top right-hand corner. I'm not sure whether it was admitted as an exhibit or not. We can look into that but we don't have a B/C/S version available to us right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D326, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have ten minutes to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you interview General Milovanovic in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in assisting in the interview of General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you put questions to General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did put questions to General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this interview take place before you compiled your report for this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the -- yes -- I'm thinking back. Yes, it did occur before I compiled my report for this case. It was when I was working for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you observe that the northern part of the line in Sarajevo was held by only one Serbian brigade, which was the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade? I'm referring to the lines fating the city proper?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think then we'd have to refer to an SRK map for me to give a conclusive answer about the coverage of the infantry brigades around Sarajevo. Is this question related to my interview with General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. So that we can see what your understanding of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is. If we orient ourselves by the river, do you agree that north of the river the line was held by only one brigade and this was the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, to answer the question, it would be much simpler to have the SRK map in front of us marked by the SRK themselves, and that would say a great deal more than ever I could say about how many brigades were facing the northern part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D01823.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the document, do you agree that in this territorial disposition in Sarajevo it was possible to use barrage fire to hinder road communications for both sides?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a technical artillery question much better directed to an artillery staff officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But wasn't it possible to use even infantry fire to hinder people moving in the Trebevic area, the Nedzarici area, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we must always remember that there was a battle going on in and around Sarajevo, and so the natural effect of artillery fire and the natural effect of mortar fire and of machine-gun fire is to hinder movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now look at this document, please, and could you read it. It's not long.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Command of the SRK. "Strictly confidential" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can read that. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, when we look at where it says "I order," is it evident that one can compile a false report and that when the front lines are so close one can pass on erroneous information purposely to the other side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I could conclude that from this document. This is -- this seems to be a request for establishment for reasons for fire having been opened on UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you can see that the commander doesn't know whether this was the case and he's asking for an investigation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be the case. That is what you would hope would happen in such situation if an event occurred that was outside the instructions that were given or that appeared to be illegal, then the commander should set up an investigation to find out what happened and why -- perhaps to prevent it from happening in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he's asking for a reliable report to be sent to the corps command. Do you accept that because of this sort of hearsay I frequently spoke very sharply to my officers, and then later on it transpired that the Serbian army had done no such thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for that conclusion we would need the actual report itself rather than the request for a report to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your chart do you agree that some things should be corrected? For example, you said that the 4th MAP consisted of batteries. It should actually be artillery battalions, which then consisted of batteries?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly agree that the charts I've produced are not complete, not perfectly correct. And I think any additional correction to them could only assist the Court, provided that those additions and corrections were backed up by documents that were reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where it says the 4th MAP T12, that artillery piece ought to belong to the 4th Mixed Anti-armour Regiment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that it would be unusual to find a T12, which after all is an anti-tank weapon, in the 4th MAP, more likely to be in the 4th Mixed Anti-Armour Regiment. I could refer to the document, if that would assist the Court, that made me put the T12 in the position I did. But it's -- in a sense may not be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there is a difference between the organisational structure and the functional organisation for ad hoc tasks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An order of battle is put together to command and control a set of units, but there are times when during battle that that organisational structure needs to be adjusted and changed. And so the charts shown are only a snap-shot, if you like, of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps over a period of time. If we were to have a chart showing the actual structure on each day, we might find each chart to be subtly different -- not very different, but we would need hundreds of charts to represent the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps over the full period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you agree then that the groups for road repairs, and so on, are not formations, but they are functionally organised to carry out certain tasks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be parts of -- if here we're talking of engineering, there may be parts of the organisation that are shown on the chart and were administered and controlled, but which in reality functioned under command perhaps of a brigade commander or slightly differently. So perhaps you might think of part of the chart showing the administrative structure of the SRK. Certainly that would be the case under engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, thanks to Mr. Reid, was an exhibit in the Galic case again and we do have the B/C/S version. And if I can refer to the prior document, I can now confirm that that was also an exhibit in the Galic case and we also have the B/C/S for that one as well. No objection to the admission of either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we will admit both of the documents, removing the marked for identification nature of the previous document. Yes. This will be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D327, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So Exhibit D326 has been admitted. So you conclude, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It appears that you spoke very highly of the theoretical knowledge of the command officers, but would you agree that things are easy to write down on paper but difficult to have implemented in practice?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's always a difference between good staff work and well-prepared analysis and well-prepared orders and the ability to carry them out. However, it does appear from the reports going up and down the chain of command from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that not only were the staff good at analysing what was occurring, good at preparing instructions and orders, but also good at ensuring that those instructions and orders were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you do agree that up until the end of the war there was this objection that there weren't enough specialised people, professionals; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. There was certainly a shortage of specialist officers. It does not appear to have prevented the corps from functioning as regards communications, engineering, and use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have no more time, then that was my final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, you have some questions for your re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. If you want to take the break first. It will only be 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, before you commence your re-examination, just one or two matters I'd like to raise with the witness, and then of course you can incorporate those matters in your re-examination, if necessary. Just to -- this is really just to outline the -- your experience and expertise to underscore the basis upon which you drew your -- constructed the charts that we have. I think there's sometimes a misunderstanding that intelligence corps officers are really James Bonds, when, in fact, the reality is - and I think you started off by telling us - you would have started off with basic infantry training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My first training was within the officers' training corps in university, and I spent four years doing simple basic military training using what was then called the common military syllabus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basic infantry tactics, shooting, living in the field. And then after four years I went to the military academy at Sandhurst where I was again trained to be an infantry officer, as all officers are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And I think a lot of intelligence corps officers are then seconded as subletons [phoen] to infantry battalions as platoon commanders in effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. In my case I spent some months previously with the Gulf Stream [phoen] Guards and so then didn't have a detachment as a territorial army officer. And so I went -- was commissioned straight into an intelligence corps battalion, as an intelligence corps officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And the function of the intelligence corps, and you will correct me if I'm wrong, really, I mean, the main purpose is collating and analysing information and interpreting it for dissemination to whoever needs it for the purposes of whatever military activity they're engaged in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a precise description of the combat intelligence part of an intelligence corps officer's job, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And I anticipate that you would have -- there's a counter-intelligence element which would include security intelligence and protective security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. For three years I was a company commander of the counter-intelligence company, then re-named to a military intelligence company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: All of -- the essential part of that is still analysis and interpretation of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. Very much of the work going on, for example, in a counter-insurgency situation is about detailing what the enemy might do next. So it's the same sort of analysis whether it's counter-analysis or combat intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And within that you would be utilising human intelligence, signal intelligence, electronic intelligence, and imagery, presumably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. A whole series of data collected using as many means as possible including reconnaissance from our own troops, as well as satellite imagery and the like, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And you had 21 years of experience as that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All together 21 years as a territorial army officer, so that's 21 years, not full-time service, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, but culminating in discharging your duties in the rank of lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left as an acting lieutenant-colonel, to be technical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I can have 65 ter 11789.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Philipps, Mr. Karadzic said to you - and this is at lines -- transcript page 3791 at line 2 - "during our interview Mr. Philipps said himself that everyone was semicircled by somebody else." And then further down on that same page at line 12 Judge Kwon asked you to confirm this and to confirm "what Mr. Karadzic just said." And you said "yes." Using -- with the assistance of the map in front of you, can you clarify what you mean when you say that everyone was semicircled by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the map on the screen, we can see around the outside of the circle on the left there's a large red line that forms a -- almost a square, but more of a triangle, and that is the operation area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and you can see that it says "SRK" in Cyrillic in the centre there. That is the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. If we look to the north-west we can see that that boundary is up against a DK, which is the Drina Corps. So that is, in fact, a safe boundary, if you like, not a boundary against the enemy. But then we can follow the direction of the lines which travel from the north and all the way down to the south around Sarajevo and then all the way to the bottom of the rectangular shape. And you can see that on one side the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is facing the ABiH, and yet on the -- to the inside there is a pocket with Sarajevo. So in my response to Mr. Karadzic I was really talking about the external lines of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and you can see that both sides have pockets where they're enveloped by one side and Sarajevo itself forms a larger pocket within the inside of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: For the record, this is map 24 of the Prosecution map book. I tender that map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1021, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If I can ask Mr. Registrar for D235.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: This was a document that Mr. Karadzic discussed with you earlier today. It's dated from April 1993 and it's entitled "Analysis of the combat-readiness and activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992." Sorry, it looks like it's the wrong document before us. I believe it's D235. It was 65 ter 01781.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 325.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is D325 -- no, D325. It was admitted today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1781.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That's correct. If we can have the English as well, please. Thank you. And if we can turn to page 28 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You can see there, Mr. Philipps, at the bottom at the section 1.1.6, Signal Units, this is the subsection that Mr. Karadzic took you to today. He precisely took you to -- if we can turn to page 35, and do you recognise that Mr. Karadzic asked you questions today about subsection C, Wire Service?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we looked at earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Now, turning over the page to page 36, which is a continuation of that same subsection, can you see at the bottom of the first paragraph the sentence reading: "A positive example of fully operational wire communications from the corps command to the first front line positions is in the SRK"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I found that now. Yes. It's just it's been overtyped in some way: "Example of a fully operational wire communications from the corps command to the first front line positions is in the SRK."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And is that consistent with your conclusions about the functioning of the chain of information and command in the SRK?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to confirm that they were able to communicate effectively up and down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And we see there in the middle of the page 1.1.6.6, Conclusions, being the conclusions of this subsection. And if we can turn over the page to page 41, and the end of those conclusions at the very top of the page reads: "I judge the combat-readiness of the signals system and corps for 1992 to have been VERY GOOD." Again, is that consistent with the conclusions that you drew?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that follows what I said earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Turning to the front of this report dealing with the VRS generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 7 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And this is the introduction entitled "Control and Command." And if we look down to the fifth paragraph starting with the sentence: "During the past year, the Army of Republika Srpska has been under a single control and command structure, despite the fact that initially we had a large number of different armies and paramilitary formations." And if you can read to yourself the remainder of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Still within the same introduction under "Control and Command," and if we look at the second paragraph and the final sentence of that paragraph reads: "The involvement of different Main Staff bodies in the brigades and other units yielded particularly good results because in that way directives, commands, and orders reached those who were to execute them in the fastest possible way, and the planned concerted action was relatively quickly performed." And if we go to the bottom of that page, the final paragraph reading: "Irrespective of the aggravating circumstances and factors which adversely affected the morale of fighters and units, we stress that on the whole it has been good and stable," and turning the page, "despite the difficulties imposed by the war, so that control and command echelons can count on it for the execution of pending missions." Again, is that consistent with your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The analysis of the Main Staff appears to be consistent with the reporting up and down the chain of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And finally, with respect to this document, if we can turn to page 152 of the English, we see there this section is entitled "Concluding Remarks, the findings of the analysis of the combat-readiness and activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992." If we turn over the page, can you see there, Mr. Philipps, who is the signatory of this report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "supreme commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if you can read the paragraph number 4 beginning: "The Supreme Command as a whole, as well as every individual member of the Supreme Command ...," if you can read that to yourself.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And again, is that consistent with the conclusions you drew about the command function of the VRS or a corps within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's consistent with my view of the functioning, the good functioning of the command and control within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 3797 at line 8, Mr. Karadzic put it to you that in the beginning the SRK "inherited only the armed people," and you responded that if that was the case then "don't -- you don't then understand where the military equipment listed came from." And you asked: "Did the Territorial Defence hold artillery?" And Mr. Karadzic responded to you: "Well, you should know that." Mr. Philipps, yesterday - and this was at page 3747, lines 8 to 11 - you spoke about the relationship between the JNA 4th Corps and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, saying: "In a sense the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was formed from the remnants of the 4th Corps of the JNA." Now, when you say that the SRK was formed from the remnants of the 4th Corps, do you know what happened to the equipment of the JNA 4th Corps, particularly their weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some knowledge of that. Some of the weapons of the 4th Corps were then into the hands of what became the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and some equipment was removed when the 4th Corps of the JNA was required to leave Sarajevo. So not all of the equipment of the 4th Corps became that of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, but a large quantity did. I have no knowledge of what equipment came from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if I can ask us to turn to Sanction and play a very short clip. This is 65 ter 45013, and we're beginning the clip at timer 00.31.17. And for the record this is a clip from a larger documentary entitled "Serbian Epics," and I believe that this clip is dated around July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We're not receiving any sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we expecting some sound, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. We appear to be having some technical difficulties. When I checked this clip this morning, it did have sound. I'm not sure whether it's the way it's been uploaded or whether it's something to do with the system in the courtroom. If we're unable to resolve those technical difficulties, then we might leave that clip. Your Honours, that concludes my re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayden. Can you bring up the map 24 which was admitted as P1021. That's my question for the witness. That's the exhibit number, P1021. I don't remember the 65 ter number. Yes. Can we blow up -- zoom it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was difficult for me to find out what is what. With the assistance of Mr. Usher, could you draw in coloured pen the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red is good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's area of responsibility, irrespective of actual confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The area of responsibility of a corps extends beyond the boundaries of where the enemy are located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we can change the colour into blue then. Could you mark the -- draw a line where the ABiH held the territory.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you continue southern direction.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's as far as the boundary line goes, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we can continue beyond the boundary -- beyond the area of responsibility of Sarajevo-Romanija --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, sort of adopt that, yeah. Does that help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And to the northern direction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not sure where the line -- I assume that the line continues that way, but that would be a surmise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused with the right -- the blue line in the right part. How does it continue, out towards -- outside the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map doesn't show. So the area, if you like, bounded by the red line and inside the blue line where the Cyrillic SRK is shown is that area actually occupied by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. It didn't necessarily have troops in every part of that, but that's where -- that's the area of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that it covered. And this map doesn't show the continuation of the lines in either direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have no knowledge about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would be guessing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you sign this document and today's date is, I take it, the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, the circle drawn in here is the zone of exclusion of heavy weapons, so heavy weapons within that circle were under the supervision of the UN, and if the interpreter can translate that we have two exclusion areas, one around Gorazde and one around Sarajevo and these are the two circles shown here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was able to read from the title of this document it's a mark of the 20-kilometre zone from the centre of Sarajevo. Whether or not it is the exclusion zone, do you agree with it, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the map post-dating the establishment of the total exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Philipps. Unless there's any further questions, that concludes -- that will be exhibited as Court exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit C1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your testimony, Mr. Philipps. Thank you for your coming to the Tribunal to give it, and now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Tieger, there's no further Prosecution witness for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. With the Court's permission, I wanted to address two matters the Court raised yesterday, and that was with respect to what the Court termed the subject of the addition of the 65 ter exhibits, asking two questions about that. Number one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have received your filing already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But yesterday, Your Honour, you also asked about the English translations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- I promised I would respond to that. And you also asked about our position with respect to the exhibit and presumably the translations too in connection with an upcoming witness. So I did want to respond to both of those in addition to the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, with respect to the translation of that proposed addition in its entirety, I did check for the most current information. That projection is for the first week of July, and that's the current information. We hope it turns out to be accurate, but it certainly can provide the Court with a generalised indication. Second, with respect to our position regarding translations in connection with the upcoming witness, I would note that despite the fact that the translation in its entirety is expected in the first week of July, that those portions of the exhibit which relate to this particular witness and to the time-period about which he's expected to give evidence have been translated and disclosed. And so that -- that issue would appear to have been resolved with respect to that particular witness. I would also note, as the Court may have had an opportunity to observe with respect to our submission today, that we were prepared to identify for the Defence, to the extent we are aware, excerpts from the proposed exhibit that refer to the witness or refer to meetings which the witness attended. And in connection with that, I took a look at the number of pages that seem to be implicated by that. I count a total of approximately 21 pages. I would also note that because of the format of the exhibit that the pages -- the number of words per page are far less than you would normally see in a document, in a classical document like a book or a report, perhaps 20 to 25 per cent, maybe a third. So it's even a smaller number. So while I don't want to be held to the precise number of pages, I think that's a pretty fair indication of the limited amount of material we're talking about with respect to that witness in particular or meetings that witness attended. I thought that might be of assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take that into account when considering the motion. As for the sitting schedule next week, we will be sitting only for three days in that week?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Albeit in one way or another in an extended format?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll tell you how the Chamber is going to sit during those three days on Monday, then that said, we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, one more matter, if I may, I'm sorry, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't mean to interrupt, I just thought you were going to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had indicated that we would get the list of Assembly sessions to you this week. I'm sorry that for technical reasons we did not. We have that ready now. I don't know how the Court wishes to deal with that. Perhaps the most efficient way is for us to provide those either between now and Monday or first thing Monday and then we can go through the tendering process on Monday or at some convenient time. But I just wanted to let the Court know that that hadn't slipped from our memory and that we can submit that list at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then Monday, 9.00, we'll resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.24 p.m.,
